title: [2605.30140] AnomalyAgent: Training-Free Agentic Models for Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection

sections.heading: AnomalyAgent: Training-Free Agentic Models for Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection

content.text: Benefiting from generalizability of vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP, many zero-/few-shot anomaly detection (AD) approaches have achieved impressive detection performance across various datasets. Nevertheless, they require substantial training on large auxiliary datasets to adapt VLMs to anomaly detection, and their inference largely relies on visual–text embedding similarity-based anomaly scores, lacking reasoning abilities to detect complex anomalies that require in-depth contextual understanding. To address this limitation, we propose AnomalyAgent, a novel training-free, agentic framework that leverages the advanced reasoning and generalization capabilities of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for anomaly detection. The key ingredients include 1) a comprehensive anomaly-centric toolset that enables adaptive MLLM-driven, agentic anomaly reasoning in zero-shot settings, and 2) a customized memory module that grounds anomaly reasoning with few-shot, in-context reference examples. We extend evaluation beyond the detection of simple anomalies (e.g., surface defects like cracks and dents and clear legions) in widely used benchmarks to more diverse types of anomalies such as logical/contextual anomalies in logistics and manufacturing settings. Extensive experiment results demonstrate that our AnomalyAgent achieves substantially better performance compared to training-free VLM-based AD and generic agentic methods, highlighting its superior generalization capability in both zero-shot and few-shot anomaly detection settings. The code implementation can be find at [this address](https://github.com/mala-lab/AnomalyAgent).

Anomaly detection (AD) is one key task in computer vision, aiming to identify instances that deviate significantly from the underlying data distribution. It is critical for a wide range of real-world applications, including industrial inspection, medical diagnosis, security monitoring, and autonomous systems Bergmann et al. ([2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib42 "MVTec ad–a comprehensive real-world dataset for unsupervised anomaly detection")); Salehi et al. ([2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib50 "Multiresolution knowledge distillation for anomaly detection")); Bergmann et al. ([2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib66 "Beyond dents and scratches: logical constraints in unsupervised anomaly detection and localization")); Höfer et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib64 "Kaputt: a large-scale dataset for visual defect detection")). A key challenge in AD lies in its inherent open-ended nature, ie, anomalies are rare, diverse and often unpredictable, making it impractical to exhaustively model all possible abnormalites during training. To tackle this challenge, conventional approaches Pang et al. ([2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib59 "Deep learning for anomaly detection: a review")); Cao et al. ([2024a](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib1 "A survey on visual anomaly detection: challenge, approach, and prospect")); Wu et al. ([2026](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib2 "Deep learning for video anomaly detection: a review")) focus on learning normal patterns from large normal training data instead. Recent advances have shifted from this unsupervised learning paradigm toward data-efficient settings, particularly zero-shot Xu et al. ([2026](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib68 "MRAD: zero-shot anomaly detection with memory-driven retrieval")); Fang et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib32 "AF-clip: zero-shot anomaly detection via anomaly-focused clip adaptation")); Cao et al. ([2024b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib30 "Adaclip: adapting clip with hybrid learnable prompts for zero-shot anomaly detection")) and few-shot AD Qu et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib77 "Dictas: a framework for class-generalizable few-shot anomaly segmentation via dictionary lookup")); Zhang et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib71 "Towards training-free anomaly detection with vision and language foundation models")); Jeong et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib26 "Winclip: zero-/few-shot anomaly classification and segmentation")), depending on the availability of normal reference samples.

Benefiting from the strong zero/few-shot recognition capabilities of pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs), a line of work has emerged to adapt their unified visual-text representations for AD via parameter-efficient tuning, achieving impressive performance across multiple benchmarks Zhou et al. ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib29 "AnomalyCLIP: object-agnostic prompt learning for zero-shot anomaly detection")); Zhu et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib36 "Fine-grained abnormality prompt learning for zero-shot anomaly detection")); Ma et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib31 "Aa-clip: enhancing zero-shot anomaly detection via anomaly-aware clip")). Early studies such as WinCLIP Jeong et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib26 "Winclip: zero-/few-shot anomaly classification and segmentation")) establish a training-free paradigm by exploiting handcrafted text prompts and multi-scale visual features from CLIP Zheng et al. ([2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib22 "Generative and contrastive self-supervised learning for graph anomaly detection")) for anomaly scoring, providing strong baselines for zero- and few-shot AD.

Following this direction, zero-shot AD methods typically enhance visual–text alignment via prompt learning to capture anomaly-relevant semantics Zhu et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib36 "Fine-grained abnormality prompt learning for zero-shot anomaly detection")); Zhou et al. ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib29 "AnomalyCLIP: object-agnostic prompt learning for zero-shot anomaly detection")); Cao et al. ([2024b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib30 "Adaclip: adapting clip with hybrid learnable prompts for zero-shot anomaly detection")); Ma et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib31 "Aa-clip: enhancing zero-shot anomaly detection via anomaly-aware clip")), while few-shot AD methods leverage normal reference samples to characterize expected normal patterns and detect anomalies through reference-based comparison with query samples Zhu and Pang ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib67 "Toward generalist anomaly detection via in-context residual learning with few-shot sample prompts")); Chen et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib27 "April-gan: a zero-/few-shot anomaly classification and segmentation method for cvpr 2023 vand workshop challenge tracks 1&2: 1st place on zero-shot ad and 4th place on few-shot ad")); Qu et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib77 "Dictas: a framework for class-generalizable few-shot anomaly segmentation via dictionary lookup")).

However, existing VLM-based methods still require substantial training on auxiliary datasets to adapt the VLMs to AD. Furthermore, their inference largely rely on visual–text representation similarity-based anomaly scoring, which provides only shallow alignment between text prompts and visual features, with anomalies identified via thresholding of the resulting scores Xu et al. ([2026](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib68 "MRAD: zero-shot anomaly detection with memory-driven retrieval")); Roth et al. ([2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib78 "Towards total recall in industrial anomaly detection")). While effective for relatively simple and well-defined anomaly patterns, such as surface defects or localized lesions, this paradigm lacks explicit reasoning, making it insufficient for handling anomalies that require contextual, relational, or task-specific understanding. For example, detection of logical anomalies may depend on object arrangement or operational rules Bergmann et al. ([2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib66 "Beyond dents and scratches: logical constraints in unsupervised anomaly detection and localization")); Zhang et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib71 "Towards training-free anomaly detection with vision and language foundation models")), while real-world industrial and logistics scenarios often exhibit open-ended variations in object appearance, pose and environmental conditions Höfer et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib64 "Kaputt: a large-scale dataset for visual defect detection")).

These challenges go beyond shallow representation matching and require more structured reasoning about such contextual and logical abnormalities. Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer a promising foundation for such reasoning and beyond Bai et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib79 "Qwen technical report")); Liu et al. ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib81 "Deepseek-v3 technical report")); Li et al. ([2024a](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib80 "Llava-onevision: easy visual task transfer")). However, their application to the AD task remains largely underexplored. Existing MLLM-based AD methods typically use reasoning either for anomaly interpretation Jiang et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib72 "MMAD: a comprehensive benchmark for multimodal large language models in industrial anomaly detection")); Xu et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib73 "Towards zero-shot anomaly detection and reasoning with multimodal large language models")); Chao et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib74 "Anomalyr1: a grpo-based end-to-end mllm for industrial anomaly detection")); Gu et al. ([2024b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib84 "AnomalyGPT: detecting industrial anomalies using large vision-language models")), or as auxiliary prior extraction for downstream anomaly analysis Zhang et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib71 "Towards training-free anomaly detection with vision and language foundation models")). In both cases, MLLM reasoning is not directly integrated into the detection decision itself, restricting its utility for zero-shot and few-shot AD. As a consequence, their effectiveness in zero-shot and few-shot anomaly detection settings remains limited, often underperforming strong VLM-based training-free baselines or requiring dataset-specific tuning to achieve competitive performance.

To address these challenges, we propose AnomalyAgent, a fully training-free agentic framework that directly leverages the superior agentic abilities of MLLMs—planning, tool use, reasoning, and reflecting—specifically for anomaly detection. As illustrated in Fig. [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ AnomalyAgent: Training-Free Agentic Models for Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection"), unlike existing VLM-based methods that rely on shallow similarity matching with auxiliary-domain tuning, or previous MLLM-based approaches that require task-specific adaptation for post-hoc reasoning, AnomalyAgent directly integrates anomaly-centric agentic abilities into the detection process itself in a fully training-free manner. To this end, an anomaly-centric toolset is introduced in AnomalyAgent to progressively gather and verify visual evidence through hypothesis-driven exploration, counterfactual verification, and reflective reasoning tailored for AD. This allows it to handle complex abnormality patterns beyond simple appearance deviations. In scenarios where in-context examples are available, e.g., few-shot AD settings, a self calibration-based memory mechanism is further introduced to convert the few-shot examples into actionable in-context memories to enable self calibration of the reasoning against dataset-specific normal patterns in AnomalyAgent.
Overall, our contributions are summarized as follows:

* • We introduce AnomalyAgent, a novel training-free agentic framework tailored for AD. It shifts anomaly detection from visual-text representation similarity-based anomaly scoring to tool-and-memory-augmented anomaly reasoning,enabling score-thresholding-free anomaly decision and in-depth reasoning over complex abnormality patterns. * • We further propose an anomaly-centric reasoning toolset and a self calibration-based memory mechanism to build an agentic AD-oriented planning–reasoning–reflecting pipeline. With this pipeline, AnomalyAgent can actively gather, verify, and refine evidence against expected normal patterns throughout its reasoning, and bring in external memories to perform self calibration when such information is available. * • We establish a comprehensive evaluation benchmark covering a wide range of anomaly types across multiple AD scenarios, including industrial inspection, medical imaging, and logistics. Extensive comparisons with VLM-based methods and MLLM agents demonstrate the strong generalization ability of AnomalyAgent in both zero-shot and few-shot settings.

We introduce AnomalyAgent, a novel training-free agentic framework tailored for AD. It shifts anomaly detection from visual-text representation similarity-based anomaly scoring to tool-and-memory-augmented anomaly reasoning,enabling score-thresholding-free anomaly decision and in-depth reasoning over complex abnormality patterns.

We further propose an anomaly-centric reasoning toolset and a self calibration-based memory mechanism to build an agentic AD-oriented planning–reasoning–reflecting pipeline. With this pipeline, AnomalyAgent can actively gather, verify, and refine evidence against expected normal patterns throughout its reasoning, and bring in external memories to perform self calibration when such information is available.

We establish a comprehensive evaluation benchmark covering a wide range of anomaly types across multiple AD scenarios, including industrial inspection, medical imaging, and logistics. Extensive comparisons with VLM-based methods and MLLM agents demonstrate the strong generalization ability of AnomalyAgent in both zero-shot and few-shot settings.

VLM-based Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection. To improve generalization to unseen domains, zero- and few-shot anomaly detection (ZSAD/FSAD) methods have emerged to identify anomalies without dataset-specific training. Recent advances are largely driven by vision-language models (VLMs), which enable AD through visual–text similarity matching in a unified embedding space. Early methods such as WinCLIP Jeong et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib26 "Winclip: zero-/few-shot anomaly classification and segmentation")) establish a training-free paradigm by exploiting CLIP Radford et al. ([2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib38 "Learning transferable visual models from natural language supervision")) features with handcrafted prompts under both ZSAD and FSAD settings. For ZSAD, subsequent approaches mainly improve anomaly-sensitive representation learning through prompt-based adaptation Chen et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib27 "April-gan: a zero-/few-shot anomaly classification and segmentation method for cvpr 2023 vand workshop challenge tracks 1&2: 1st place on zero-shot ad and 4th place on few-shot ad")); Zhu et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib36 "Fine-grained abnormality prompt learning for zero-shot anomaly detection")); Zhou et al. ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib29 "AnomalyCLIP: object-agnostic prompt learning for zero-shot anomaly detection")); Cao et al. ([2024b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib30 "Adaclip: adapting clip with hybrid learnable prompts for zero-shot anomaly detection")); Gu et al. ([2024a](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib34 "Filo: zero-shot anomaly detection by fine-grained description and high-quality localization")). For example, APRIL-GAN Chen et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib27 "April-gan: a zero-/few-shot anomaly classification and segmentation method for cvpr 2023 vand workshop challenge tracks 1&2: 1st place on zero-shot ad and 4th place on few-shot ad")) introduces additional learnable layers trained with auxiliary anomaly data, while methods such as AnomalyCLIP Zhou et al. ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib29 "AnomalyCLIP: object-agnostic prompt learning for zero-shot anomaly detection")), FAPrompt Zhu et al. For FSAD, existing methods leverage normal reference samples through reference-based comparison Li et al. ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib82 "ResAD: a simple framework for class generalizable anomaly detection")). PromptAD Li et al. ([2024b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib83 "PromptAD: learning prompts with only normal samples for few-shot anomaly detection")) learns class-specific normal patterns via one-class prompt learning, while InCTRL Zhu and Pang ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib67 "Toward generalist anomaly detection via in-context residual learning with few-shot sample prompts")) and ResAD Yao et al. ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib82 "ResAD: a simple framework for class generalizable anomaly detection")) model residual discrepancies between query samples and normal references for anomaly detection. However, these methods still rely on similarity-based decision mechanisms, limiting their effectiveness in scenarios requiring contextual or relational understanding.

MLLM-based Anomaly Detection and Reasoning. Motivated by the strong reasoning capability of MLLMs, recent studies explore anomaly detection from a reasoning perspective. Approaches such as MMAD Jiang et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib72 "MMAD: a comprehensive benchmark for multimodal large language models in industrial anomaly detection")), AnomalyGPT Gu et al. ([2024b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib84 "AnomalyGPT: detecting industrial anomalies using large vision-language models")), Anomaly-OV Xu et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib73 "Towards zero-shot anomaly detection and reasoning with multimodal large language models")), and AnomalyR1 Chao et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib74 "Anomalyr1: a grpo-based end-to-end mllm for industrial anomaly detection")) mainly treat MLLMs as post-hoc reasoning modules for anomaly analysis through natural language descriptions or multi-step inference. Other methods, such as LogSAD Zhang et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib71 "Towards training-free anomaly detection with vision and language foundation models")), leverage MLLMs to model structural or logical constraints as prior knowledge for AD. However, existing methods still lack anomaly-aware reasoning guidance that explicitly integrates reasoning into the anomaly detection process itself, often requiring dataset-specific tuning and underperforming strong training-free VLM baselines. Recent agentic frameworks have demonstrated strong capabilities in planning, tool use, and multi-step reasoning across multimodal tasks Yao et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib69 "REACT: synergizing reasoning and acting in language models")); Shinn et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib70 "Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning")); Chhikara et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib76 "Mem0: building production-ready ai agents with scalable long-term memory")). However, directly applying generic agents to AD remains challenging due to the lack of anomaly-specific reasoning guidance and calibrated normality priors. In contrast, AnomalyAgent is a fully training-free agentic AD framework that explicitly integrates MLLM reasoning into anomaly detection through an anomaly-centric reasoning toolset and a self-calibration-based memory mechanism.

Overview of AnomalyAgent. As illustrated in Fig. [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Anomaly-Centric Toolset for AD-Oriented Agentic Planning–Reasoning–Reflecting ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ AnomalyAgent: Training-Free Agentic Models for Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection"), AnomalyAgent inputs the image and the class name into the template tools, deriving the general template analysis and class-specific counterfactual template analysis. Given the general template analysis and the raw image, the Planner selects and invokes an appropriate visual tool to enhance anomaly-relevant evidence. Then, the augmented image, raw image, and template analysis are fed into the Reasoner for judgment. If the termination condition is not met, the aforementioned information, as well as the Reasoner’s thought, will be input into the Reflector for a new loop of investigation. Below, we present these modules in detail.

children.heading: 3.1 Anomaly-Centric Toolset for AD-Oriented Agentic Planning–Reasoning–Reflecting

content.text: To enable anomaly detection in a fully training-free setting, we present a zero-shot agentic framework that can adapt to diverse inspection requirements without accessing training samples or performing parameter updates. Unlike generic MLLM agents that mainly rely on open-ended visual question answering, AnomalyAgent is specifically designed for anomaly detection from two complementary aspects: an anomaly-centric toolset that provides task-relevant visual and semantic evidence, and an AD-oriented agentic pipeline that progressively plans, reasons, and reflects over such evidence before making a hard-label prediction.

The tools in AnomalyAgent are organized into two categories. The first category consists of general visual tools, which enhance the query image or focus on local regions to provide clearer visual evidence for anomaly inspection. The second category consists of template tools, which exploit both textual priors and image-level descriptions to construct structured anomaly-related cues. This design enables the agent to improve the visibility of suspicious observations while grounding its reasoning in explicit AD-specific priors.

General Visual Tools. We include five general visual tools: image denoising, image deblurring, super-resolution, zooming, and brightness adjustment. These tools are invoked when the Planner or the Reflector identifies insufficient or ambiguous visual evidence, such as low image quality, small suspicious regions, blur, or poor illumination. The implementations are provided in the Appendix [A.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#A1.SS1 "A.1 Details of Visual Tool Use ‣ Appendix A More Implmentation Details ‣ AnomalyAgent: Training-Free Agentic Models for Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection").

To verify the effectiveness of AnomalyAgent, we conduct extensive experiments across five real-world datasets from diverse application domains, including industrial defect dataset (MVTec Bergmann et al. ([2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib42 "MVTec ad–a comprehensive real-world dataset for unsupervised anomaly detection"))), medical image datasets (HeadCT Salehi et al. ([2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib50 "Multiresolution knowledge distillation for anomaly detection")) and LAG Li et al. ([2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib51 "Attention based glaucoma detection: a large-scale database and cnn model"))), logistics defect dataset (Kaputt Höfer et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib64 "Kaputt: a large-scale dataset for visual defect detection"))), and logical anomaly dataset (MVTec LOCO Bergmann et al. ([2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib66 "Beyond dents and scratches: logical constraints in unsupervised anomaly detection and localization"))). These are test datasets, which are used directly to evaluate the detection performance in the zero-shot setting. In the few-shot setting, the few-shot normal prompts for the target data are randomly sampled from the training set of target datasets and remain the same for all detection models for fair comparison. We evaluate the performance with varying number of few-shot normal sample set: K=1,2,4K=1,2,4 (See Appendix for details about the dataset settings).

We compare AnomalyAgent with several state-of-the-art (SotA) anomaly detection methods under both zero-shot and few-shot settings. For ZSAD, the competing methods include training-free baselines, ie, CLIP Radford et al. ([2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib38 "Learning transferable visual models from natural language supervision")), WinCLIP Jeong et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib26 "Winclip: zero-/few-shot anomaly classification and segmentation")), MRAD Xu et al. ([2026](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib68 "MRAD: zero-shot anomaly detection with memory-driven retrieval")), and ReAct Agent Yao et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib69 "REACT: synergizing reasoning and acting in language models")). We also include trainable ZSAD approaches, including APRIL-GAN Chen et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib27 "April-gan: a zero-/few-shot anomaly classification and segmentation method for cvpr 2023 vand workshop challenge tracks 1&2: 1st place on zero-shot ad and 4th place on few-shot ad")), AnomalyCLIP Zhou et al. ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib29 "AnomalyCLIP: object-agnostic prompt learning for zero-shot anomaly detection")), and FAPrompt Zhu et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib36 "Fine-grained abnormality prompt learning for zero-shot anomaly detection")), but they are not included for direct performance comparison; their results are only used to check the performance gap between training-free and trainable AD methods. For FSAD, the training-free baselines include WinCLIP+ Jeong et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib26 "Winclip: zero-/few-shot anomaly classification and segmentation")), PatchCore Roth et al. ([2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib78 "Towards total recall in industrial anomaly detection")), and an agentic method Mem0 Chhikara et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib76 "Mem0: building production-ready ai agents with scalable long-term memory")), while the trainable baselines include APRIL-GAN Chen et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib27 "April-gan: a zero-/few-shot anomaly classification and segmentation method for cvpr 2023 vand workshop challenge tracks 1&2: 1st place on zero-shot ad and 4th place on few-shot ad")) and InCTRL Zhu and Pang ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib67 "Toward generalist anomaly detection via in-context residual learning with few-shot sample prompts")). Note that ReAct is not included in the FSAD experiments as it cannot directly use the few-shot references; similarly, Mem0 that requires few-shot references is not used in the ZSAD experiments. Following previous AD approaches Cao et al. ([2024b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib30 "Adaclip: adapting clip with hybrid learnable prompts for zero-shot anomaly detection")); Zhang et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib71 "Towards training-free anomaly detection with vision and language foundation models")); Fučka et al. ([2026](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib86 "AnomalyVFM–transforming vision foundation models into zero-shot anomaly detectors")), we report the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (AUROC) and the highest possible F1 score (F1-max) as our evaluation metrics.

We use GPT-5.1 OpenAI ([2025b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib87 "GPT-5.1")) with the Response API as the default MLLM for all agentic methods (AnomalyAgent, ReACT, and Mem0) for image description, planning, reasoning, and reflection in the main experiments. To reduce inference cost, GPT-4.1-mini OpenAI ([2025a](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib88 "GPT-4.1 mini")) is used for auxiliary reasoning and memory-related operations. For embedding-based evidence matching, we employ a Qwen3-4B-based text embedding model Yang and others ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib89 "Qwen3 technical report")) by default. For training-free methods, all datasets are directly used for inference without any training or adaptation. For trainable methods, we follow the official experimental protocols of the competing approaches, where models are trained on their corresponding auxiliary datasets and evaluated on the target test sets without further fine-tuning. Implementation details for AnomalyAgent and the competing methods are provided in Appendix.

Zero-shot Anomaly Detection. Table [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AnomalyAgent: Training-Free Agentic Models for Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection") reports the ZSAD results across five datasets for both fully training-free and trainable methods. Overall, AnomalyAgent achieves the best average performance among all training-free methods, surpassing the strongest training-free baseline by up to 2.7% AUROC and 1.7% F1F\_{1}-max\max. Compared with conventional VLM-based approaches relying on visual–language similarity matching, AnomalyAgent shows particularly strong improvements on datasets requiring contextual and relational understanding, such as MVTec LOCO and Kaputt, and even achieves competitive performance against several trainable methods. Although trainable approaches such as AnomalyCLIP and FAPrompt still obtain slightly better results on some datasets due to auxiliary-domain optimization, AnomalyAgent remains highly competitive without any training or parameter adaptation. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed agentic reasoning framework for handling contextual, structural, and task-dependent anomalies.

As for the generic MLLM agent ReAct, it achieves competitive performance compared with WinCLIP, demonstrating the potential of agentic reasoning for AD. However, a clear gap still exists between ReAct and AnomalyAgent, suggesting that generic MLLM agents lack AD-specific reasoning guidance and calibrated normality priors for reliable anomaly understanding. In contrast, AnomalyAgent explicitly organizes anomaly-centric tools within a structured reasoning workflow, enabling more reliable anomaly decisions across diverse AD scenarios. Moreover, the consistently stronger F1F\_{1}-max\max results achieved by MLLM-based methods, particularly ReAct and AnomalyAgent, indicate that reasoning-based anomaly analysis produces more discriminative anomaly decisions with better normal/anomaly separation than conventional anomaly scoring-based methods.

Few-shot Anomaly Detection. Table [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AnomalyAgent: Training-Free Agentic Models for Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection") reports the 1-, 2-, and 4-shot AD results. Among training-free baselines, AnomalyAgent achieves the best performance in the majority of dataset–shot settings and consistently obtains the highest average AUROC and F1F\_{1}-max\max across all shot numbers, surpassing the strongest training-free baseline by up to 2.8% AUROC and 2.5% F1F\_{1}-max\max. Similar trends to the zero-shot setting can also be observed for both VLM-based and MLLM-based methods. Compared with conventional VLM-based FSAD methods, AnomalyAgent shows particularly strong improvements on datasets requiring contextual and relational understanding, while generic MLLM agents still exhibit clear limitations due to the lack of AD-specific reasoning guidance and calibrated normality priors. More importantly, AnomalyAgent exhibits stable cross-shot improvement, with performance consistently increasing from 1-shot to 4-shot. In contrast, Mem0, which equips the zero-shot version of AnomalyAgent with a generic memory module, does not reliably benefit from additional shots. This suggests that the advantage of AnomalyAgent comes not merely from memory augmentation, but from an AD-specific memory mechanism that transforms few-shot normal references into effective in-context normality priors for reasoning calibration. Although trainable methods such as InCTRL still achieve slightly stronger performance through AD-specific optimization, AnomalyAgent remains highly competitive without any training or parameter adaptation, further validating the effectiveness of memory-calibrated agentic reasoning for FSAD.

Ablation Study. In this section, we analyze the key design choices in AnomalyAgent under both zero-shot and few-shot settings. Unless otherwise specified, GPT-4.1-mini is adopted as the default MLLM throughout this analysis for efficiency considerations.

Table [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Analysis of AnomalyAgent ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AnomalyAgent: Training-Free Agentic Models for Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection") presents the ablation results on MVTec and MVTec LOCO. Under the zero-shot setting, the ‘Base’ model, which only contains the Planner and Reasoner, achieves limited performance, especially on the challenging dataset MVTec LOCO, where structural consistency and category-level priors are more critical. Introducing reflective reasoning (‘w. Ref.’) only leads to marginal improvements, suggesting that reasoning loops alone are insufficient without additional AD-related evidence or external guidance. Further incorporating general visual tools (i.e., ‘w. Ref. & V-Tools’) significantly improves the performance on MVTec, demonstrating the importance of enhanced visual evidence for the detection of simple anomalies. However, the performance on MVTec LOCO slightly drops, indicating that general visual processing alone is insufficient for the detection of complex anomalies, e.g., logical anomalies in MVTec LOCO. In contrast, AnomalyAgent (the zero-shot version) consistently achieves the best performance across both datasets under the zero-shot setting, suggesting that the proposed anomaly-centric toolset provides valuable anomaly priors for effective detection of both simple and complex anomalies. This also indicate that such toolset should be explicitly integrated into the reasoning workflow rather than treated as optional tools.

For the few-shot setting, all variants are built upon the zero-shot version of AnomalyAgent. The variant ‘w. Hard-Normal’ injects hard-normal information extracted from the few-shot normal references, while ‘w. Calibration’ uses few-shot samples to calibrate the cross-modal prior tools toward the target-data normal patterns. It is clear that using hard-normal information alone leads to only limited improvements (‘w. Hard-Normal’ vs. the zero-shot AnomalyAgent), suggesting that simply providing additional normal descriptions is insufficient for effective few-shot anomaly reasoning. In contrast, the calibration variant achieves consistently stronger performance, indicating that few-shot samples are more effective when used to adapt anomaly reasoning toward the target-data normal distribution. Finally, integrating both hard-normal information and calibration into AnomalyAgent (i.e., the few-shot AnomalyAgent) yields the best overall performance, demonstrating that explicit normality priors and memory-calibrated reasoning are complementary for few-shot anomaly detection.

Hyperparameter Sensitivity. AnomalyAgent contains two key hyperparameters: KK, which controls the number of selected atomic candidates in counterfactual template analysis, and NN, which denotes the number of consecutive ‘Normal’ judgments required for agent termination. Fig. [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Analysis of AnomalyAgent ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AnomalyAgent: Training-Free Agentic Models for Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection") presents the corresponding hyperparameter sensitivity analysis on MVTec and MVTec LOCO. As shown in Fig. [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Analysis of AnomalyAgent ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AnomalyAgent: Training-Free Agentic Models for Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection")(a), the performance first improves and then slightly drops as KK increases. A small KK may provide insufficient anomaly-relevant evidence for reliable reasoning, while an overly large KK can introduce redundant or noisy candidates that weaken the discriminability of the counterfactual analysis. Overall, AnomalyAgent achieves the best trade-off around K=5K=5. Fig. [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Analysis of AnomalyAgent ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AnomalyAgent: Training-Free Agentic Models for Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection")(b) analyzes the effect of NN. Increasing NN from 1 to 3 consistently improves the performance, suggesting that requiring multiple consecutive normal judgments helps suppress premature normal predictions and leads to more reliable anomaly decisions. However, further increasing NN to 4 slightly degrades the performance, possibly because excessive confirmation introduces over-conservative reasoning behavior. Finally, Fig. [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Analysis of AnomalyAgent ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AnomalyAgent: Training-Free Agentic Models for Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection")(c) compares different MLLM backbones. Larger and stronger MLLMs consistently lead to improved anomaly detection performance, verifying that the proposed reasoning framework can effectively benefit from stronger multimodal reasoning capability.

This work introduces AnomalyAgent, offering a principled agentic framework that unleashes the superior reasoning abilities of MLLMs for training-free zero- and few-shot AD. This is not viable to the generic agentic models due to the lack of anomaly-centric priors and normality. To tackle this challenge, two novel components, including a comprehensive anomaly-centric toolset and self calibration-based memory mechanism, are introduced in AnomalyAgent. Our extensive experiments show that, with the support of these two components, AnomalyAgent achieves promising zero- and few-shot AD performance, significantly outperforming training-free VLM-based AD models and generic MLLM-based agents, with competitive performance to SotA trainable VLM-based methods.

children.heading: A.1 Details of Visual Tool Use

content.text: AnomalyAgent equips the MLLM agent with a set of lightweight visual tools to support anomaly-oriented evidence gathering. These tools provide complementary observations under different visual conditions, and their outputs are not used as standalone anomaly predictions. Instead, the processed observations are returned to the planner–reasoner–reflector loop, where they are considered together with the original image, semantic priors, counterfactual evidence, and accumulated reasoning history. All tools are invoked only at inference time and do not require target-dataset training or parameter adaptation.

The denoising tool is implemented with OpenCV’s fast non-local means filtering, which suppresses color and spatial noise while preserving local image structures. In AnomalyAgent, this tool is useful when suspected defects may be confused with acquisition noise, compression artifacts, or low-light degradation, allowing the reasoner to verify whether the abnormal evidence remains visible after noise suppression.

The deblurring tool is implemented with unsharp masking based on Gaussian blur subtraction. It enhances local edges and contours without introducing any learned adaptation. This tool is used when anomaly hypotheses depend on boundary sharpness, object shape, or surface discontinuities, helping the agent distinguish true structural irregularities from blur-induced ambiguity.

The brightness enhancement tool applies contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization (CLAHE) to the L-channel in the LAB color space. This operation improves local contrast while limiting over-amplification. In the reasoning loop, it is used to re-examine regions affected by under-exposure or over-exposure, where abnormal patterns may otherwise be hidden or visually exaggerated.

The super-resolution tool uses Real-ESRGAN Wang et al. ([2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib90 "Real-esrgan: training real-world blind super-resolution with pure synthetic data")) to enhance image resolution and recover fine-grained texture details. This provides additional visual evidence for cases where the anomaly decision relies on small defects, subtle texture changes, or local missing components. The enhanced image is treated as an auxiliary observation for verification rather than as a replacement for the original image.

The retrieval tool uses CLIP-based visual-textual retrieval Radford et al. ([2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib38 "Learning transferable visual models from natural language supervision")), where cosine similarity between CLIP embeddings is used to score relevance. This tool provides contextual reference evidence by retrieving previously observed examples related to the current query or suspected abnormal pattern. The retrieved results are used to support comparison with normal or suspicious visual patterns, but the final anomaly decision is still made by the reasoner through the agentic reasoning process.

chunks.text:
###### Abstract

Benefiting from generalizability of vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP, many zero-/few-shot anomaly detection (AD) approaches have achieved impressive detection performance across various datasets. Nevertheless, they require substantial training on large auxiliary datasets to adapt VLMs to anomaly detection, and their inference largely relies on visual–text embedding similarity-based anomaly scores, lacking reasoning abilities to detect complex anomalies that require in-depth contextual understanding. To address this limitation, we propose AnomalyAgent, a novel training-free, agentic framework that leverages the advanced reasoning and generalization capabilities of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for anomaly detection. The key ingredients include 1) a comprehensive anomaly-centric toolset that enables adaptive MLLM-driven, agentic anomaly reasoning in zero-shot settings, and 2) a customized memory module that grounds anomaly reasoning with few-shot, in-context reference examples. We extend evaluation beyond the detection of simple anomalies (e.g., surface defects like cracks and dents and clear legions) in widely used benchmarks to more diverse types of anomalies such as logical/contextual anomalies in logistics and manufacturing settings. Extensive experiment results demonstrate that our AnomalyAgent achieves substantially better performance compared to training-free VLM-based AD and generic agentic methods, highlighting its superior generalization capability in both zero-shot and few-shot anomaly detection settings. The code implementation can be find at [this address](https://github.com/mala-lab/AnomalyAgent).

## 1 Introduction

Anomaly detection (AD) is one key task in computer vision, aiming to identify instances that deviate significantly from the underlying data distribution. It is critical for a wide range of real-world applications, including industrial inspection, medical diagnosis, security monitoring, and autonomous systems Bergmann et al. ([2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib42 "MVTec ad–a comprehensive real-world dataset for unsupervised anomaly detection")); Salehi et al. ([2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib50 "Multiresolution knowledge distillation for anomaly detection")); Bergmann et al. ([2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib66 "Beyond dents and scratches: logical constraints in unsupervised anomaly detection and localization")); Höfer et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib64 "Kaputt: a large-scale dataset for visual defect detection")). A key challenge in AD lies in its inherent open-ended nature, ie, anomalies are rare, diverse and often unpredictable, making it impractical to exhaustively model all possible abnormalites during training. To tackle this challenge, conventional approaches Pang et al. ([2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib59 "Deep learning for anomaly detection: a review")); Cao et al. ([2024a](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib1 "A survey on visual anomaly detection: challenge, approach, and prospect")); Wu et al. ([2026](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib2 "Deep learning for video anomaly detection: a review")) focus on learning normal patterns from large normal training data instead. Recent advances have shifted from this unsupervised learning paradigm toward data-efficient settings, particularly zero-shot Xu et al. ([2026](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib68 "MRAD: zero-shot anomaly detection with memory-driven retrieval")); Fang et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib32 "AF-clip: zero-shot anomaly detection via anomaly-focused clip adaptation")); Cao et al. ([2024b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib30 "Adaclip: adapting clip with hybrid learnable prompts for zero-shot anomaly detection")) and few-shot AD Qu et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib77 "Dictas: a framework for class-generalizable few-shot anomaly segmentation via dictionary lookup")); Zhang et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib71 "Towards training-free anomaly detection with vision and language foundation models")); Jeong et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib26 "Winclip: zero-/few-shot anomaly classification and segmentation")), depending on the availability of normal reference samples.

Benefiting from the strong zero/few-shot recognition capabilities of pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs), a line of work has emerged to adapt their unified visual-text representations for AD via parameter-efficient tuning, achieving impressive performance across multiple benchmarks Zhou et al. ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib29 "AnomalyCLIP: object-agnostic prompt learning for zero-shot anomaly detection")); Zhu et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib36 "Fine-grained abnormality prompt learning for zero-shot anomaly detection")); Ma et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib31 "Aa-clip: enhancing zero-shot anomaly detection via anomaly-aware clip")). Early studies such as WinCLIP Jeong et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib26 "Winclip: zero-/few-shot anomaly classification and segmentation")) establish a training-free paradigm by exploiting handcrafted text prompts and multi-scale visual features from CLIP Zheng et al. ([2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib22 "Generative and contrastive self-supervised learning for graph anomaly detection")) for anomaly scoring, providing strong baselines for zero- and few-shot AD.

Following this direction, zero-shot AD methods typically enhance visual–text alignment via prompt learning to capture anomaly-relevant semantics Zhu et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib36 "Fine-grained abnormality prompt learning for zero-shot anomaly detection")); Zhou et al. ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib29 "AnomalyCLIP: object-agnostic prompt learning for zero-shot anomaly detection")); Cao et al. ([2024b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib30 "Adaclip: adapting clip with hybrid learnable prompts for zero-shot anomaly detection")); Ma et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib31 "Aa-clip: enhancing zero-shot anomaly detection via anomaly-aware clip")), while few-shot AD methods leverage normal reference samples to characterize expected normal patterns and detect anomalies through reference-based comparison with query samples Zhu and Pang ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib67 "Toward generalist anomaly detection via in-context residual learning with few-shot sample prompts")); Chen et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib27 "April-gan: a zero-/few-shot anomaly classification and segmentation method for cvpr 2023 vand workshop challenge tracks 1&2: 1st place on zero-shot ad and 4th place on few-shot ad")); Qu et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib77 "Dictas: a framework for class-generalizable few-shot anomaly segmentation via dictionary lookup")).

However, existing VLM-based methods still require substantial training on auxiliary datasets to adapt the VLMs to AD. Furthermore, their inference largely rely on visual–text representation similarity-based anomaly scoring, which provides only shallow alignment between text prompts and visual features, with anomalies identified via thresholding of the resulting scores Xu et al. ([2026](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib68 "MRAD: zero-shot anomaly detection with memory-driven retrieval")); Roth et al. ([2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib78 "Towards total recall in industrial anomaly detection")). While effective for relatively simple and well-defined anomaly patterns, such as surface defects or localized lesions, this paradigm lacks explicit reasoning, making it insufficient for handling anomalies that require contextual, relational, or task-specific understanding. For example, detection of logical anomalies may depend on object arrangement or operational rules Bergmann et al. ([2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib66 "Beyond dents and scratches: logical constraints in unsupervised anomaly detection and localization")); Zhang et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib71 "Towards training-free anomaly detection with vision and language foundation models")), while real-world industrial and logistics scenarios often exhibit open-ended variations in object appearance, pose and environmental conditions Höfer et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib64 "Kaputt: a large-scale dataset for visual defect detection")).

These challenges go beyond shallow representation matching and require more structured reasoning about such contextual and logical abnormalities. Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer a promising foundation for such reasoning and beyond Bai et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib79 "Qwen technical report")); Liu et al. ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib81 "Deepseek-v3 technical report")); Li et al. ([2024a](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib80 "Llava-onevision: easy visual task transfer")). However, their application to the AD task remains largely underexplored. Existing MLLM-based AD methods typically use reasoning either for anomaly interpretation Jiang et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib72 "MMAD: a comprehensive benchmark for multimodal large language models in industrial anomaly detection")); Xu et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib73 "Towards zero-shot anomaly detection and reasoning with multimodal large language models")); Chao et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib74 "Anomalyr1: a grpo-based end-to-end mllm for industrial anomaly detection")); Gu et al. ([2024b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib84 "AnomalyGPT: detecting industrial anomalies using large vision-language models")), or as auxiliary prior extraction for downstream anomaly analysis Zhang et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib71 "Towards training-free anomaly detection with vision and language foundation models")). In both cases, MLLM reasoning is not directly integrated into the detection decision itself, restricting its utility for zero-shot and few-shot AD. As a consequence, their effectiveness in zero-shot and few-shot anomaly detection settings remains limited, often underperforming strong VLM-based training-free baselines or requiring dataset-specific tuning to achieve competitive performance.

To address these challenges, we propose AnomalyAgent, a fully training-free agentic framework that directly leverages the superior agentic abilities of MLLMs—planning, tool use, reasoning, and reflecting—specifically for anomaly detection. As illustrated in Fig. [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ AnomalyAgent: Training-Free Agentic Models for Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection"), unlike existing VLM-based methods that rely on shallow similarity matching with auxiliary-domain tuning, or previous MLLM-based approaches that require task-specific adaptation for post-hoc reasoning, AnomalyAgent directly integrates anomaly-centric agentic abilities into the detection process itself in a fully training-free manner. To this end, an anomaly-centric toolset is introduced in AnomalyAgent to progressively gather and verify visual evidence through hypothesis-driven exploration, counterfactual verification, and reflective reasoning tailored for AD. This allows it to handle complex abnormality patterns beyond simple appearance deviations. In scenarios where in-context examples are available, e.g., few-shot AD settings, a self calibration-based memory mechanism is further introduced to convert the few-shot examples into actionable in-context memories to enable self calibration of the reasoning against dataset-specific normal patterns in AnomalyAgent.

Overall, our contributions are summarized as follows:

* • We introduce AnomalyAgent, a novel training-free agentic framework tailored for AD. It shifts anomaly detection from visual-text representation similarity-based anomaly scoring to tool-and-memory-augmented anomaly reasoning,enabling score-thresholding-free anomaly decision and in-depth reasoning over complex abnormality patterns. * • We further propose an anomaly-centric reasoning toolset and a self calibration-based memory mechanism to build an agentic AD-oriented planning–reasoning–reflecting pipeline. With this pipeline, AnomalyAgent can actively gather, verify, and refine evidence against expected normal patterns throughout its reasoning, and bring in external memories to perform self calibration when such information is available. * • We establish a comprehensive evaluation benchmark covering a wide range of anomaly types across multiple AD scenarios, including industrial inspection, medical imaging, and logistics. Extensive comparisons with VLM-based methods and MLLM agents demonstrate the strong generalization ability of AnomalyAgent in both zero-shot and few-shot settings.

## 2 Related Work

VLM-based Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection. To improve generalization to unseen domains, zero- and few-shot anomaly detection (ZSAD/FSAD) methods have emerged to identify anomalies without dataset-specific training. Recent advances are largely driven by vision-language models (VLMs), which enable AD through visual–text similarity matching in a unified embedding space. Early methods such as WinCLIP Jeong et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib26 "Winclip: zero-/few-shot anomaly classification and segmentation")) establish a training-free paradigm by exploiting CLIP Radford et al. ([2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib38 "Learning transferable visual models from natural language supervision")) features with handcrafted prompts under both ZSAD and FSAD settings. For ZSAD, subsequent approaches mainly improve anomaly-sensitive representation learning through prompt-based adaptation Chen et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib27 "April-gan: a zero-/few-shot anomaly classification and segmentation method for cvpr 2023 vand workshop challenge tracks 1&2: 1st place on zero-shot ad and 4th place on few-shot ad")); Zhu et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib36 "Fine-grained abnormality prompt learning for zero-shot anomaly detection")); Zhou et al. ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib29 "AnomalyCLIP: object-agnostic prompt learning for zero-shot anomaly detection")); Cao et al. ([2024b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib30 "Adaclip: adapting clip with hybrid learnable prompts for zero-shot anomaly detection")); Gu et al. ([2024a](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib34 "Filo: zero-shot anomaly detection by fine-grained description and high-quality localization")). For example, APRIL-GAN Chen et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib27 "April-gan: a zero-/few-shot anomaly classification and segmentation method for cvpr 2023 vand workshop challenge tracks 1&2: 1st place on zero-shot ad and 4th place on few-shot ad")) introduces additional learnable layers trained with auxiliary anomaly data, while methods such as AnomalyCLIP Zhou et al. ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib29 "AnomalyCLIP: object-agnostic prompt learning for zero-shot anomaly detection")), FAPrompt Zhu et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib36 "Fine-grained abnormality prompt learning for zero-shot anomaly detection")), and AdaCLIP Cao et al. ([2024b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib30 "Adaclip: adapting clip with hybrid learnable prompts for zero-shot anomaly detection")) employ learnable prompts to better align visual features with anomaly-relevant semantics. For FSAD, existing methods leverage normal reference samples through reference-based comparison Li et al. ([2024b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib83 "PromptAD: learning prompts with only normal samples for few-shot anomaly detection")); Zhu and Pang ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib67 "Toward generalist anomaly detection via in-context residual learning with few-shot sample prompts")); Yao et al. ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib82 "ResAD: a simple framework for class generalizable anomaly detection")). PromptAD Li et al. ([2024b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib83 "PromptAD: learning prompts with only normal samples for few-shot anomaly detection")) learns class-specific normal patterns via one-class prompt learning, while InCTRL Zhu and Pang ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib67 "Toward generalist anomaly detection via in-context residual learning with few-shot sample prompts")) and ResAD Yao et al. ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib82 "ResAD: a simple framework for class generalizable anomaly detection")) model residual discrepancies between query samples and normal references for anomaly detection. However, these methods still rely on similarity-based decision mechanisms, limiting their effectiveness in scenarios requiring contextual or relational understanding.

MLLM-based Anomaly Detection and Reasoning. Motivated by the strong reasoning capability of MLLMs, recent studies explore anomaly detection from a reasoning perspective. Approaches such as MMAD Jiang et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib72 "MMAD: a comprehensive benchmark for multimodal large language models in industrial anomaly detection")), AnomalyGPT Gu et al. ([2024b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib84 "AnomalyGPT: detecting industrial anomalies using large vision-language models")), Anomaly-OV Xu et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib73 "Towards zero-shot anomaly detection and reasoning with multimodal large language models")), and AnomalyR1 Chao et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib74 "Anomalyr1: a grpo-based end-to-end mllm for industrial anomaly detection")) mainly treat MLLMs as post-hoc reasoning modules for anomaly analysis through natural language descriptions or multi-step inference. Other methods, such as LogSAD Zhang et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib71 "Towards training-free anomaly detection with vision and language foundation models")), leverage MLLMs to model structural or logical constraints as prior knowledge for AD. However, existing methods still lack anomaly-aware reasoning guidance that explicitly integrates reasoning into the anomaly detection process itself, often requiring dataset-specific tuning and underperforming strong training-free VLM baselines. Recent agentic frameworks have demonstrated strong capabilities in planning, tool use, and multi-step reasoning across multimodal tasks Yao et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib69 "REACT: synergizing reasoning and acting in language models")); Shinn et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib70 "Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning")); Chhikara et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib76 "Mem0: building production-ready ai agents with scalable long-term memory")). However, directly applying generic agents to AD remains challenging due to the lack of anomaly-specific reasoning guidance and calibrated normality priors. In contrast, AnomalyAgent is a fully training-free agentic AD framework that explicitly integrates MLLM reasoning into anomaly detection through an anomaly-centric reasoning toolset and a self-calibration-based memory mechanism.

### 3.1 Anomaly-Centric Toolset for AD-Oriented Agentic Planning–Reasoning–Reflecting

To enable anomaly detection in a fully training-free setting, we present a zero-shot agentic framework that can adapt to diverse inspection requirements without accessing training samples or performing parameter updates. Unlike generic MLLM agents that mainly rely on open-ended visual question answering, AnomalyAgent is specifically designed for anomaly detection from two complementary aspects: an anomaly-centric toolset that provides task-relevant visual and semantic evidence, and an AD-oriented agentic pipeline that progressively plans, reasons, and reflects over such evidence before making a hard-label prediction.

#### Anomaly-Centric Toolset.

The tools in AnomalyAgent are organized into two categories. The first category consists of general visual tools, which enhance the query image or focus on local regions to provide clearer visual evidence for anomaly inspection. The second category consists of template tools, which exploit both textual priors and image-level descriptions to construct structured anomaly-related cues. This design enables the agent to improve the visibility of suspicious observations while grounding its reasoning in explicit AD-specific priors.

General Visual Tools. We include five general visual tools: image denoising, image deblurring, super-resolution, zooming, and brightness adjustment. These tools are invoked when the Planner or the Reflector identifies insufficient or ambiguous visual evidence, such as low image quality, small suspicious regions, blur, or poor illumination. The implementations are provided in the Appendix [A.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#A1.SS1 "A.1 Details of Visual Tool Use ‣ Appendix A More Implmentation Details ‣ AnomalyAgent: Training-Free Agentic Models for Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection").

#### Datasets.

To verify the effectiveness of AnomalyAgent, we conduct extensive experiments across five real-world datasets from diverse application domains, including industrial defect dataset (MVTec Bergmann et al. ([2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib42 "MVTec ad–a comprehensive real-world dataset for unsupervised anomaly detection"))), medical image datasets (HeadCT Salehi et al. These are test datasets, which are used directly to evaluate the detection performance in the zero-shot setting. In the few-shot setting, the few-shot normal prompts for the target data are randomly sampled from the training set of target datasets and remain the same for all detection models for fair comparison. #### Baseline Methods and Evaluation Metrics.

We compare AnomalyAgent with several state-of-the-art (SotA) anomaly detection methods under both zero-shot and few-shot settings. For ZSAD, the competing methods include training-free baselines, ie, CLIP Radford et al. ([2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib38 "Learning transferable visual models from natural language supervision")), WinCLIP Jeong et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib26 "Winclip: zero-/few-shot anomaly classification and segmentation")), MRAD Xu et al. ([2026](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib68 "MRAD: zero-shot anomaly detection with memory-driven retrieval")), and ReAct Agent Yao et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib69 "REACT: synergizing reasoning and acting in language models")). We also include trainable ZSAD approaches, including APRIL-GAN Chen et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib27 "April-gan: a zero-/few-shot anomaly classification and segmentation method for cvpr 2023 vand workshop challenge tracks 1&2: 1st place on zero-shot ad and 4th place on few-shot ad")), AnomalyCLIP Zhou et al. ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib29 "AnomalyCLIP: object-agnostic prompt learning for zero-shot anomaly detection")), and FAPrompt Zhu et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib36 "Fine-grained abnormality prompt learning for zero-shot anomaly detection")), but they are not included for direct performance comparison; their results are only used to check the performance gap between training-free and trainable AD methods. For FSAD, the training-free baselines include WinCLIP+ Jeong et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib26 "Winclip: zero-/few-shot anomaly classification and segmentation")), PatchCore Roth et al. ([2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib78 "Towards total recall in industrial anomaly detection")), and an agentic method Mem0 Chhikara et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib76 "Mem0: building production-ready ai agents with scalable long-term memory")), while the trainable baselines include APRIL-GAN Chen et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib27 "April-gan: a zero-/few-shot anomaly classification and segmentation method for cvpr 2023 vand workshop challenge tracks 1&2: 1st place on zero-shot ad and 4th place on few-shot ad")) and InCTRL Zhu and Pang ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib67 "Toward generalist anomaly detection via in-context residual learning with few-shot sample prompts")). Note that ReAct is not included in the FSAD experiments as it cannot directly use the few-shot references; similarly, Mem0 that requires few-shot references is not used in the ZSAD experiments. Following previous AD approaches Cao et al. ([2024b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib30 "Adaclip: adapting clip with hybrid learnable prompts for zero-shot anomaly detection")); Zhang et al. ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib71 "Towards training-free anomaly detection with vision and language foundation models")); Fučka et al. ([2026](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib86 "AnomalyVFM–transforming vision foundation models into zero-shot anomaly detectors")), we report the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (AUROC) and the highest possible F1 score (F1-max) as our evaluation metrics.

#### Implementation Details.

We use GPT-5.1 OpenAI ([2025b](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib87 "GPT-5.1")) with the Response API as the default MLLM for all agentic methods (AnomalyAgent, ReACT, and Mem0) for image description, planning, reasoning, and reflection in the main experiments. To reduce inference cost, GPT-4.1-mini OpenAI ([2025a](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib88 "GPT-4.1 mini")) is used for auxiliary reasoning and memory-related operations. For embedding-based evidence matching, we employ a Qwen3-4B-based text embedding model Yang and others ([2025](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib89 "Qwen3 technical report")) by default. For training-free methods, all datasets are directly used for inference without any training or adaptation. For trainable methods, we follow the official experimental protocols of the competing approaches, where models are trained on their corresponding auxiliary datasets and evaluated on the target test sets without further fine-tuning. Implementation details for AnomalyAgent and the competing methods are provided in Appendix.

Under the zero-shot setting, the ‘Base’ model, which only contains the Planner and Reasoner, achieves limited performance, especially on the challenging dataset MVTec LOCO, where structural consistency and category-level priors are more critical. Introducing reflective reasoning (‘w. Ref.’) only leads to marginal improvements, suggesting that reasoning loops alone are insufficient without additional AD-related evidence or external guidance. Further incorporating general visual tools (i.e., ‘w. Ref. & V-Tools’) significantly improves the performance on MVTec, demonstrating the importance of enhanced visual evidence for the detection of simple anomalies. However, the performance on MVTec LOCO slightly drops, indicating that general visual processing alone is insufficient for the detection of complex anomalies, e.g., logical anomalies in MVTec LOCO. In contrast, AnomalyAgent (the zero-shot version) consistently achieves the best performance across both datasets under the zero-shot setting, suggesting that the proposed anomaly-centric toolset provides valuable anomaly priors for effective detection of both simple and complex anomalies. This also indicate that such toolset should be explicitly integrated into the reasoning workflow rather than treated as optional tools.

For the few-shot setting, all variants are built upon the zero-shot version of AnomalyAgent. The variant ‘w. Hard-Normal’ injects hard-normal information extracted from the few-shot normal references, while ‘w. Calibration’ uses few-shot samples to calibrate the cross-modal prior tools toward the target-data normal patterns. It is clear that using hard-normal information alone leads to only limited improvements (‘w. Hard-Normal’ vs. the zero-shot AnomalyAgent), suggesting that simply providing additional normal descriptions is insufficient for effective few-shot anomaly reasoning. In contrast, the calibration variant achieves consistently stronger performance, indicating that few-shot samples are more effective when used to adapt anomaly reasoning toward the target-data normal distribution. Finally, integrating both hard-normal information and calibration into AnomalyAgent (i.e., the few-shot AnomalyAgent) yields the best overall performance, demonstrating that explicit normality priors and memory-calibrated reasoning are complementary for few-shot anomaly detection.

Hyperparameter Sensitivity. AnomalyAgent contains two key hyperparameters: KK, which controls the number of selected atomic candidates in counterfactual template analysis, and NN, which denotes the number of consecutive ‘Normal’ judgments required for agent termination. Fig. [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Analysis of AnomalyAgent ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AnomalyAgent: Training-Free Agentic Models for Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection") presents the corresponding hyperparameter sensitivity analysis on MVTec and MVTec LOCO. As shown in Fig. [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Analysis of AnomalyAgent ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AnomalyAgent: Training-Free Agentic Models for Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection")(a), the performance first improves and then slightly drops as KK increases. A small KK may provide insufficient anomaly-relevant evidence for reliable reasoning, while an overly large KK can introduce redundant or noisy candidates that weaken the discriminability of the counterfactual analysis. Overall, AnomalyAgent achieves the best trade-off around K=5K=5. Fig. [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Analysis of AnomalyAgent ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AnomalyAgent: Training-Free Agentic Models for Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection")(b) analyzes the effect of NN. Increasing NN from 1 to 3 consistently improves the performance, suggesting that requiring multiple consecutive normal judgments helps suppress premature normal predictions and leads to more reliable anomaly decisions. ## 5 Conclusion

This work introduces AnomalyAgent, offering a principled agentic framework that unleashes the superior reasoning abilities of MLLMs for training-free zero- and few-shot AD. This is not viable to the generic agentic models due to the lack of anomaly-centric priors and normality. To tackle this challenge, two novel components, including a comprehensive anomaly-centric toolset and self calibration-based memory mechanism, are introduced in AnomalyAgent. Our extensive experiments show that, with the support of these two components, AnomalyAgent achieves promising zero- and few-shot AD performance, significantly outperforming training-free VLM-based AD models and generic MLLM-based agents, with competitive performance to SotA trainable VLM-based methods.

### A.1 Details of Visual Tool Use

AnomalyAgent equips the MLLM agent with a set of lightweight visual tools to support anomaly-oriented evidence gathering. These tools provide complementary observations under different visual conditions, and their outputs are not used as standalone anomaly predictions. Instead, the processed observations are returned to the planner–reasoner–reflector loop, where they are considered together with the original image, semantic priors, counterfactual evidence, and accumulated reasoning history. All tools are invoked only at inference time and do not require target-dataset training or parameter adaptation.

heading_path: AnomalyAgent: Training-Free Agentic Models for Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection
A.1 Details of Visual Tool Use
chunks.text:
#### Image Denoising.

The denoising tool is implemented with OpenCV’s fast non-local means filtering, which suppresses color and spatial noise while preserving local image structures. In AnomalyAgent, this tool is useful when suspected defects may be confused with acquisition noise, compression artifacts, or low-light degradation, allowing the reasoner to verify whether the abnormal evidence remains visible after noise suppression.

heading_path: AnomalyAgent: Training-Free Agentic Models for Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection
A.1 Details of Visual Tool Use
chunks.text:
#### Image Deblurring.

The deblurring tool is implemented with unsharp masking based on Gaussian blur subtraction. It enhances local edges and contours without introducing any learned adaptation. This tool is used when anomaly hypotheses depend on boundary sharpness, object shape, or surface discontinuities, helping the agent distinguish true structural irregularities from blur-induced ambiguity.

heading_path: AnomalyAgent: Training-Free Agentic Models for Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection
A.1 Details of Visual Tool Use
chunks.text:
#### Brightness Enhancement.

The brightness enhancement tool applies contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization (CLAHE) to the L-channel in the LAB color space. This operation improves local contrast while limiting over-amplification. In the reasoning loop, it is used to re-examine regions affected by under-exposure or over-exposure, where abnormal patterns may otherwise be hidden or visually exaggerated.

heading_path: AnomalyAgent: Training-Free Agentic Models for Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection
A.1 Details of Visual Tool Use
chunks.text:
#### Image Super-Resolution.

The super-resolution tool uses Real-ESRGAN Wang et al. ([2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib90 "Real-esrgan: training real-world blind super-resolution with pure synthetic data")) to enhance image resolution and recover fine-grained texture details. This provides additional visual evidence for cases where the anomaly decision relies on small defects, subtle texture changes, or local missing components. The enhanced image is treated as an auxiliary observation for verification rather than as a replacement for the original image.

heading_path: AnomalyAgent: Training-Free Agentic Models for Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection
A.1 Details of Visual Tool Use
chunks.text:
#### Image Retrieval.

The retrieval tool uses CLIP-based visual-textual retrieval Radford et al. ([2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2605.30140#bib.bib38 "Learning transferable visual models from natural language supervision")), where cosine similarity between CLIP embeddings is used to score relevance. This tool provides contextual reference evidence by retrieving previously observed examples related to the current query or suspected abnormal pattern. The retrieved results are used to support comparison with normal or suspicious visual patterns, but the final anomaly decision is still made by the reasoner through the agentic reasoning process.
